echoes.note: 'for sin' (peri hamartias) in v.3 reproduces the Septuagint's standing phrase for the sin offering; God's sending his Son 'for sin' figurally casts Christ in the role of the Levitical purification sacrifice that 'condemns sin in the flesh.'

The Spirit enabling 'the ordinance of the law' to be 'fulfilled in us' (v.4) draws on the new-covenant promise to write the Torah on the heart, internalizing the law by divine agency rather than external command.

'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' undergirds vv.4-9: the indwelling Spirit (vv.9,11) produces obedience and 'walking according to the Spirit'; the verbal cluster Spirit-indwelling-walking-statutes is distinctive to Ezekiel.

'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live' (the dry-bones vision) lies behind v.11, where the Spirit who raised Jesus 'will also give life to your mortal bodies'; Spirit-giving-life-to-dead-bodies is the precise Ezekielian figure.
The flesh/Spirit antithesis (vv.5-9), where 'flesh' marks mortal humanity opposed to God's enduring Spirit, faintly recalls 'My Spirit will not abide in man forever, for he is flesh.'
'The spirit is alive' / God giving 'life to your mortal bodies' (vv.10-11) faintly evokes the breath of life animating dust-formed Adam, now reapplied as resurrection-life by the Spirit.

'The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace' and 'if you live after the flesh you must die... by the Spirit... you will live' (vv.6,13) reframe the covenantal life-and-death choice of Moses' exhortation set before Israel.

'Israel is my son, my firstborn' grounds the sonship/adoption language of vv.14-17; the Spirit constitutes believers as 'children of God,' transferring Israel's sonship status to those led by the Spirit.
'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the adopted-son-led-by-God motif (vv.14-15); the tender father-son relation undergirds the cry 'Abba! Father!'

'In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said, You are children of the living God' anticipates 'these are children of God' / 'we are children of God' (vv.14,16); Paul cites this very text in Romans 9:26.
'You, O LORD, are our Father' — Israel's corporate address of God as Father — stands behind the Spirit-prompted filial cry 'Abba! Father!' (v.15).
'I thought you would call me My Father and would not turn from following me' — God's hope that adopted Israel address him as Father — resonates with the adoptive cry of v.15.

The covenant formula 'I will... be your God, and you shall be my people,' realized through the indwelling Spirit (vv.9-16), faintly underlies the divine-belonging and sonship affirmed by the Spirit's testimony.

'The creation was subjected to vanity... in hope' (vv.20-22) directly invokes the curse on the ground 'because of you,' the toil, thorns, and frustrated labor of the fall; creation's bondage to decay is the Edenic curse awaiting reversal.

Creation 'subjected to vanity' (mataiotes, v.20) reuses the Septuagint's rendering of hevel ('vanity of vanities'); Qoheleth's diagnosis of the cosmos's futile, breath-like emptiness is the condition from which creation longs for release.

'I create new heavens and a new earth' is the hope toward which the groaning creation strains (vv.19-22): the liberation of creation 'into the liberty of the glory of the children of God' is the prophetic new-creation renewal of the cosmos.

The peaceable, restored creation under the messianic shoot — wolf with lamb, no harm in all God's holy mountain — anticipates creation 'delivered from the bondage of decay,' the redeemed cosmos liberated alongside God's children (vv.19-21).

'The earth mourns and withers... the earth is defiled under its inhabitants' depicts the groaning land suffering under human transgression, parallel to creation subjected to futility and groaning (vv.20-22).

'Like a woman with child... we writhed in pain' supplies the birth-pang imagery of 'the whole creation groans and travails in pain together' (v.22); creation labors toward the deliverance of new life.

Zion's travail bringing forth her children before her pain comes echoes the link between creation's birth-pangs (v.22) and the 'revealing of the children of God' / 'redemption of the body' (vv.19,23).
'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of judgment and impending deliverance resonates faintly with the cosmic travail of v.22.
'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' as eschatological down-payment resonates with 'the first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23), the Spirit as the firstfruits/guarantee of the coming redemption.
'The first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23) draws on the cultic firstfruits offering that consecrates and pledges the full harvest; the Spirit is the consecrating pledge of the redeemed body.
The lament's 'why do you sleep?... our soul is bowed down... redeem us' anticipates the groaning, waiting, and hoped-for redemption (vv.23-25); the same psalm is quoted at v.36.
'All my longing is before you; my groaning is not hidden from you' resonates with the inarticulate groaning the Spirit voices before 'him who searches the hearts' (vv.26-27).
'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds 'he who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit's mind' (v.27); God's heart-discerning gaze validates the wordless intercession.
'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' supplies the precise epithet 'he who searches the hearts' (v.27); the heart-searcher reads the Spirit's unutterable groanings.
'O LORD, you have searched me and known me... you discern my thoughts from afar' resonates with God searching the hearts and knowing the Spirit's mind (v.27).

Being 'conformed to the image of his Son' (v.29) reworks humanity's creation in the image of God; the restored image is now christological, the Son as the prototype to which the predestined are refashioned.

'I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth' grounds 'that he might be the firstborn among many brothers' (v.29); the Davidic-messianic firstborn title is extended to the Son who heads a redeemed family.
'Israel is my firstborn son' reinforces the 'firstborn among many brothers' (v.29): the firstborn-son status, once Israel's, belongs to the Son who incorporates many siblings.
'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you... I appointed you' supplies the foreknowing-and-appointing pattern of vv.29-30; divine foreknowledge as elective purpose precedes calling.
The Servant 'called from the womb,' named before birth, resonates with the chain of foreknowing, predestining, and calling in vv.29-30.
'You meant evil... but God meant it for good' faintly underlies 'all things work together for good for those who love God' (v.28); divine providence turning suffering toward good.
'Showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments' supplies the covenantal designation 'those who love God' (v.28), the loving-God-and-being-blessed pattern.

v.36 cites verbatim with the formula 'even as it is written': 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.' The lament psalm of the righteous suffering for God's sake interprets the believers' affliction (v.35).

The Servant's courtroom taunt 'He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?... It is the Lord GOD who helps me; who will declare me guilty?' is reworked into 'Who could bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns?' (vv.33-34); the forensic question-and-answer pattern is shared.

'He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' (v.32) echoes the Aqedah, where God says to Abraham 'you have not withheld (spared) your son, your only son'; God now does for all what Abraham was prepared to do, the Father not sparing his own Son.

'Because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son' reinforces v.32; the Septuagint's verb for 'spare/withhold' (pheidomai) is the same word Paul uses, strengthening the Aqedah allusion.

'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and the Servant 'delivered up' (LXX paradidomi, 53:6,12) stands behind 'delivered him up for us all' (v.32); the handing-over of the Servant for the many.

The Servant 'poured out his soul to death... bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors' resonates with Christ who 'makes intercession for us' (v.34); both join self-giving death with ongoing intercession.
'Sit at my right hand' grounds 'who is at the right hand of God' (v.34); the enthronement of the exalted Lord secures his advocacy and the impossibility of any condemnation.
'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?' supplies the rhetorical shape of 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); the same God-for-me-therefore-fearless logic.
'The LORD is with us; do not fear them' resonates with 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); divine presence nullifies opposing power.
'This I know, that God is for me' is a near-verbal antecedent to 'God is for us' (v.31), the confidence that God's siding with the petitioner routs adversaries.
'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?... though war arise against me, yet I will be confident' resonates with the catalogue of perils that cannot prevail (vv.35,37-39).
'There is no god besides me... I kill and I make alive' underlies the totalizing pairing 'neither death, nor life' (v.38) as the extremes wholly within God's sovereign love.

The catalogue of deprivations (failed crops, no flock) followed by 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD' parallels the list of hardships in v.35 that cannot separate from God's love, culminating in triumphant confidence (v.37).
The three youths' confidence that 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us' amid fire and sword resonates with believers as 'more than conquerors' through perils including 'sword' (vv.35-37).

'The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them... having been disciplined a little they will receive great good' parallels the assurance that no affliction separates from God's love (vv.35-39); the righteous tested 'like gold in the furnace' and found worthy.
'The righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord... they will receive a glorious crown' resonates with being 'more than conquerors' and inseparable from God's love (vv.37-39).

The martyr-mother and seven sons, killed 'all day long' for covenant faithfulness yet confident of resurrection, resonate with 'for your sake we are killed all day long' read as triumphant martyrdom (vv.36-37).
'In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword' enumerates perils paralleling v.35's famine, sword, and danger, with God's protection through them.
